newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. official says Afghanistan faces aid fatigue.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official says Afghanistan faces aid fatigue.

text.p: A senior U.N. official said on Monday that war-ravaged Afghanistan was a victim of global "compassion fatigue", but the world could not ignore the plight of Asia's poorest nation.

"There are too many humanitarian crises in many parts of the world," Yasushi Akashi, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, told Reuters in an interview. "There is an inevitable compassion fatigue which has sunk in."

Akashi was speaking before flying to Turkmenistan's capital, Ashgabat, for a two-day meeting at which 250 delegates from donor countries, U.N. agencies and private aid groups will discuss a unified strategy for assistance to Afghanistan.

He said a conventional approach, keeping a clear distinction between short-term relief and long-term reconstruction and rehabilitation, was not appropriate for Afghanistan, fragmented and unable to function as a state after 18 years of conflict.
"This is not any more an emergency situation," he said. "It's a protracted crisis."

Akashi said the Ashgabat meeting would take stock of how to deal with what he described as "one of the foremost crises in the world, if not the foremost crisis", despite the frustration arising from repeatedly dashed peace hopes.
"It would be an affront to the conscience of humanity if we simply ignore the situation," he declared.

The purist Islamic Taleban militia, which captured Kabul in September, made major gains against its opponents north of the Afghan capital last week, taking the Soviet-built military air base of Bagram and the town of Charikar.

It launched its offensive against forces loyal to former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood and northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum less than 24 hours after U.N.-brokered peace talks in Islamabad ended after three days without result.

"At some stage in any peace process you can use post-war reconstruction and rehabilitation as an inducement to talk seriously about peace," Akashi said. "But until that comes, the leaders are obsessed with the military situation."

He said the Ashgabad meeting should send a strong signal to warring Afghans: "If you agree to peace, we'll come up with this tremendous aid package that will assist your people. The pie is simply too small for you to fight over its division."

The carrot of humanitarian aid, even though this was offered on a non-political basis, could be used to promote peace. "We are very interested in synchronising assistance with peace negotiation," he added.

Akashi acknowledged that the arrival in power of the Taleban had complicated the task of U.N. and other aid agencies whose views on human rights, especially those of women, conflict with the movement's strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law.
"They (the Taleban) are an extremely determined ideological group, very puritanical, but sooner or later they will have to come to grips with reality," he said.
"If they are genuinely concerned for their people, half of their people are women. I am in the long run optimistic that they will accept our attitude, our policies," he said.
Akashi said this now appeared to be a minority view among U.N. and other aid officials, many of whom believed that the Taleban would not compromise on issues such as women's rights.

"There is no consensus. The majority view is...that of frustration, that of not achieving much, however much they have talked with the Taleban authorities, while there is a minority view that there is a residual pragmatism, a recognition of reality, on the part of the Taleban," Akashi said.

"We are in a dilemma," he added. "Our mission is to send humanitarian goods, basic necessities, to the victims of war and civil conflict...On the other hand, we have to adhere to certain stands, certain rules, regarding the distribution of humanitarian goods and there should be no compromise on that."
